creative.body:
I am 61, I beat breast cancer, and I want my sex life back.

If reading that sentence felt like being seen, this is for you.

I want to start with that one because every other version of this story I have read makes me feel like I have to apologize for it. Like the price of survival is supposed to be a quiet, grateful, sexless rest of my life. Like the women who really earned it are the ones who say "I am just happy to be here" and mean it all the way down.

I am happy to be here. I am also a person.

I miss my body. I miss the version of myself that did not flinch when my husband reached across the bed. I miss the easy, dumb, animal pleasure of being a woman in her own skin.

I am allowed to miss that. So are you.

I am writing this because I read a thread on Reddit at 2 in the morning, 6 months into the worst stretch of my survivorship, where a woman wrote one sentence that made me put my phone down and walk into the kitchen and cry in front of the refrigerator.

She wrote, "My sex drive as well as my partner's is way too high to let fucking cancer get in the way."

That was it. The whole post.

And I read it and I felt seen for the first time in 2 years.

Because here is what nobody tells you.

The cultural script around breast cancer survivorship is gratitude. It is pink ribbons. It is "you are lucky to be alive." It is your sister bringing you a casserole and squeezing your hand and telling you to just rest.

All of that is real. All of that is good.

None of it leaves room for the part of you that wants more than to be lucky. The part of you that wants to be a woman again.

Not a survivor. Not a fighter. Not an inspiration. A woman.

Gratitude, the way it gets used in a survivorship support group, is often a cage. It is the thing well-meaning people put around you so that you do not say the embarrassing thing out loud.

The embarrassing thing is that you are alive and you still want more. The embarrassing thing is that your sex life mattered to you before the diagnosis and it still matters to you now and you do not know how to admit that without sounding ungrateful to the people who prayed for you.

Survival is the floor. It is not the ceiling.

Gratitude and desire are not opposites. They live in the same body.

The woman who is grateful to be alive and the woman who wants her body back are the same woman, and pretending they are not is what has kept you quiet for 2 years.

The medication that is keeping you alive, if you are on an aromatase inhibitor like I am, has driven your estradiol to undetectable. That is the point. That is how it works.

Letrozole, anastrozole, exemestane. They suppress the small amount of estrogen your body still produces after menopause, because that small amount of estrogen is what feeds the kind of cancer we had.

The trade is real. The trade is also unspoken.

The trade is your sex life. The trade is the elasticity of your tissue. The trade is the bacterial balance that has kept your body working since puberty. The trade is the easy, animal feeling of being touched without bracing for it.

What I want to say to you, sitting wherever you are reading this, is that the trade is not the whole deal.

You can keep the medication and reclaim the body. The 2 are not in opposition.

The protocol your oncologist's office handed you, the Replens and the coconut oil and the lube, is not the actual standard of care. It is the polite version of the standard of care. It is what they say when they have 90 seconds and a waiting room full of women.

The actual standard of care, the one written down in the 2018 American Society of Clinical Oncology guideline and the National Comprehensive Cancer Network survivorship guideline, is a non-hormonal vaginal moisturizer used regularly.

The word that matters in that sentence is moisturizer, not lubricant. The 2 are not the same.

A moisturizer rebuilds the tissue. A lubricant covers it for the next 20 minutes.

There has not been, until very recently, a non-hormonal moisturizer that actually does what the guideline asks for.

The products on the shelf hydrate the surface. They do not address the bacterial environment that has collapsed. They do not feed the lactobacillus your body used to keep alive on its own. They do not sustain the work between doses.

For a year I thought "vaginal dryness" was one problem.

Once I read the literature I understood it is 4 problems wearing a single name.

The first thing the medication takes is the deep tissue hydration. Not surface dryness. The water content of the tissue itself, the part of you that gives elasticity and keeps the walls thick.

The second thing it takes is the lactobacillus colonies, the bacteria that keep your vagina acidic and protected and have been doing that quiet work since you were 13 years old.

The third thing it takes is the glycogen your epithelium used to make. Glycogen is the food the lactobacillus lives on. No estrogen, no glycogen. No glycogen, no bacteria.

The fourth thing it takes is the body's ability to maintain any of this on its own between interventions. Even if you put something in once, it does not stay.

When I lined that up against the products I had been told to use, the gap was almost embarrassing.

Replens hydrates the surface. That covers a fraction of the first problem and none of the other 3.

Coconut oil sits on top of the tissue and feeds the wrong bacteria, which makes the second problem worse, not better.

Lubricants are designed for the 20 minutes of intercourse. They are not addressing any of the 4.

At my next follow-up I told my oncologist what was actually happening. She looked at me kindly, the way she does, and said, "We can revisit vaginal estrogen at year 5 if you are still struggling."

I nodded. I am the kind of woman who nods.

I drove home. I sat in my own kitchen with my coat still on and I did the math.

I was 3 years out. Year 5 was 2 more years away. 2 more years of flinching when my husband reached. 2 more years of the version of myself I missed getting a little farther away each month.

I was not going to wait 2 more years for permission.

I made tea. I opened my laptop. I started looking on my own.

I want to be honest about what I felt sitting at that table. It was not anger at her. It was the small, quiet decision that nobody else was going to do this part for me.

The medical chart was not going to ask the question. So I had to.

Around then a friend who works in a survivorship support program gave me the name of a sex counselor who specializes in oncology survivorship. AASECT-certified, the real credential.

I called her. We talked for an hour.

She told me she had stopped counting how many of her clients had stopped having sex within a year of starting the AI. She said the medical system has not built the conversation around it because nobody on the prescribing side has time for it.

She said the women she sees do not need permission to want their bodies back. They need somebody to tell them out loud that wanting it is not the betrayal they have been treating it as.

I also want to talk about the niche problem, because it is the thing that almost made me give up before I found Avelle.

Once I knew estrogen was off the table for me, I started looking for products built for "women like us." What I found, over and over, was a category that had been built for general menopause and then adjusted at the edges for survivors.

A box would say "non-hormonal" and then I would read the panel and find a phytoestrogen. A product would say "for sensitive women" and then I would find DHEA in the active ingredients. A brand would say "natural" and then I would find sea buckthorn, which is exactly the kind of phytoestrogenic ingredient survivor communities have been raising flags about for years.

The whole shelf had been designed first for the larger market, and the small group of women whose oncology chart says no estrogen had been treated as a footnote.

I told myself I was probably too niche to matter.

That turned out not to be true.

The product I started using 9 months ago is called Avelle.

Avelle was not built for general menopause and adjusted at the edges for survivors. It was built first for the woman whose oncology chart says no estrogen, and the formulation choices follow from that starting point, not the other way around.

It is a vaginal suppository, used a few times a week.

The hyaluronic acid pulls water deep into the tissue. The lactobacillus lactis helps restore the healthy bacterial environment your body recognizes. The glycogen gives those bacteria the food source your body's own estrogen used to provide. The polydextrose is a prebiotic fiber that keeps the colony working over time.

Hydrate. Balance. Feed. Sustain. 4 molecules, 4 jobs, one suppository.

I read every ingredient on the box out loud, because by then I had a no-list and I was not going to take anyone's word for it.

Hyaluronic acid is a sugar molecule that holds water. It does not bind the estrogen receptor. Lactobacillus lactis is a bacterium. It is not a hormone. Glycogen is a carbohydrate. Polydextrose is a soluble fiber.

Nothing on that list is a phytoestrogen. Nothing on that list is DHEA. Nothing on that list is a hormone analog.

No estrogen. No phytoestrogens. No DHEA. No hormone analogs. No parabens. No phthalates.

There is one number from the literature I keep coming back to.

70 to 93% of women on aromatase inhibitors develop GSM symptoms. Of those, fewer than 5% are offered any treatment that meets the modern guideline definition.

I am not a doctor, and I had to read it 3 times to make sure I had the numbers right.

Almost every woman on the medication I was on. Fewer than 5 in 100 of us, offered the actual standard.

That is the gap I had been sitting inside without a name for it.

I brought the Avelle handout to my oncologist. She read 2 paragraphs and said she had no objection.

That was the entire conversation. I started it the next week.

The phrase that mattered there, and I want to underline it because it took me almost 2 years to learn it, was "no objection."

Not "approval." Not "I prescribe this." No objection.

That is the exact language an oncologist is trained to use when a patient brings her something that is consistent with the literature and outside her direct prescribing authority. It is not a shrug. It is the green light, in the only words she is allowed to give it.

I will not promise you that you will feel like yourself in the first month. I did not.

The first month was small. The pressure was a little less. The burning a little less.

By the third month I noticed that I had stopped flinching.

By the fifth month my husband and I had something close to the marriage we used to have.

I am not trying to sell you a fairy tale.

I am trying to tell you that the body you used to live in is not gone. The medication did not take it. The protocol your oncology office handed you is what was making it feel gone.

You are allowed to want your body back. You are allowed to want pleasure. You are allowed to want your marriage to feel like a marriage and not like 2 people taking care of an invalid.

You earned all of that the day they told you the margins were clean.

When I looked at the order page, I noted what was on it. Reviewed by oncologists. Per-lot third-party testing. A printable handout I could bring to my next appointment.

3 things that, for 2 years, no one in survivorship had handed me on a single product.

Now I want to say the hardest part of this letter.

There are 2 kinds of women who finish reading this. There is no third kind.

The first kind closes the tab. She tells herself the wanting is selfish. She tells herself a real survivor would be grateful enough not to ask. She lets the next 18 months look exactly like the last 18 months.

The version of herself she misses gets a little farther away each month, until it is a person she used to know rather than a person she used to be.

The second kind prints the handout. She brings it to her next appointment. She watches her oncologist read it. She listens for the sentence "I have no objection." She gives her body 4 months and finds out what her body wants to do when the 4 things the medication took are put back in.

The risk that actually matters is the wait one.

It is your husband stopping reaching first, or you stopping responding first, and neither of you remembering the order anymore. It is the slow disappearance of the woman you were before the diagnosis, not because the cancer took her, but because the polite version of the standard of care never gave her back to you.

The medication is doing what it is supposed to do. It is not going to stop. Your body is not going to stage a quiet recovery while estradiol stays undetectable.

That is not pessimism. That is the mechanism.

The wasted thing is not the box. The wasted thing is the months you keep telling yourself that wanting more is selfish.

It isn't. It never was.

When I went to order, I saw they had a 90-day money-back guarantee. I sat with that.

I had been on the patient side of an aromatase inhibitor for almost 3 years at that point, and not once in those 3 years had any pharmaceutical company offered to give me my money back if their drug did not work.

The Replens did not come with a refund offer. The coconut oil did not. The lubricants the PA had handed me did not.

The first time anyone in my survivorship had said, in writing, that if their product did not do the work they would give me my money back, was a small company I had found through a clinical trial registry.

That alone made me trust them more than the system that had handed me a tube of Replens.

I had read enough by that point to understand why they made the batches small. Lactobacillus lactis is a live culture, and the glycogen it feeds on has a finite shelf-active window once the suppository is formed. They batch-produce because they will not ship a bottle whose colony has aged out of viability sitting in a warehouse.

The trade-off is that they sell out for a few weeks at a stretch.

If they are in stock the day you click through, that is the day to order. You do not wait until next week.

If you are reading this at 2 in the morning the way I read that one-sentence Reddit post at 2 in the morning, the woman who said her sex drive was too high to let fucking cancer get in the way, then you already know what it felt like to be seen.

You are her. So am I.

The 4 months you give your body, starting this week, is the difference between the woman you used to be becoming a person you used to know, or coming back.
creative.title: I Beat Breast Cancer. I Want My Sex Life Back. Both Things Are True.
